subject: math
cluster: Reason about and solve one-variable equations and inequalities
description: Students write a one-variable inequality of the form $x > c$, $x < c$, $x \ge c$, or $x \le c$ to represent a constraint or condition from a real-world or mathematical situation, and they recognize that such inequalities have infinitely many solutions. They represent the solution set on a number line, using an open circle for strict inequalities ($>$, $<$) and a closed circle for inclusive inequalities ($\ge$, $\le$), with the shaded ray pointing toward all values that satisfy the condition.
subSkills: Translate a verbal constraint or condition into an inequality of the form $x > c$, $x < c$, $x \ge c$, or $x \le c$
Choose the correct inequality symbol from key phrases ('more than' $\to$ $>$, 'at least' $\to$ $\ge$, 'fewer than' $\to$ $<$, 'at most' $\to$ $\le$)
Recognize that an inequality like $x > c$ has infinitely many solutions rather than a single value
Graph the solution set on a number line: open circle for $>$ or $<$, closed circle for $\ge$ or $\le$
Determine the correct direction of the shaded ray (greater than shades right, less than shades left)
Read a number-line graph and write the matching inequality
Test whether a given value is a solution by substituting into the inequality

problemArchetypes.name: Verbal constraint to inequality
problemArchetypes.example: A ride requires that a passenger be at least $48$ inches tall. Writing $h$ for height in inches, the constraint is $h \ge 48$.

problemArchetypes.name: Graph a given inequality
problemArchetypes.example: Graph $x < 3$ on a number line: place an open circle at $3$ and shade the ray to the left.

problemArchetypes.name: Number line to inequality
problemArchetypes.example: A number line shows a closed circle at $-2$ with shading to the right. The inequality is $x \ge -2$.

problemArchetypes.name: Recognize infinitely many solutions
problemArchetypes.example: For $x > 5$, which describes the solutions? Answer: there are infinitely many values, every number greater than $5$.

problemArchetypes.name: Test a value / identify a solution
problemArchetypes.example: Is $x = 7$ a solution of $x \le 7$? Yes, because $7 \le 7$ is true (the closed circle includes $7$).

Easy.description: Direct one-step translation or graphing with small non-negative whole numbers and an unambiguous key phrase. Either write a strict inequality ($>$ or $<$) from clear wording, or graph a given strict inequality, or read a simple graph. No inclusive ($\ge$, $\le$) reasoning and no negatives.
constraints: Constant $c$ is a small whole number ($0$ to $20$)
Key phrase is explicit: 'greater than', 'less than', 'more than', 'fewer than'
Single step: words to symbols, symbols to graph, or graph to symbols

Medium.description: Requires distinguishing inclusive from strict inequalities ($\ge$ vs $>$, $\le$ vs $<$) from boundary phrases ('at least', 'at most', 'no more than', 'no fewer than'), or graphing with the correct open vs closed circle. May use negative constants or simple fractions/decimals for $c$, and may ask the student to identify that the solution set is infinite.
constraints: Includes $\ge$ and $\le$ cases requiring closed circles
Boundary phrases ('at least', 'at most', 'no more than') must be interpreted
Constant $c$ may be negative or a simple fraction/decimal (e.g. $-3$, $\frac{1}{2}$, $2.5$)
May require recognizing infinitely many solutions or testing a candidate value

Hard.description: Multi-step or context-rich: extract the variable and the boundary from a longer real-world scenario, decide both the symbol AND the open/closed convention AND the shading direction, or reconcile a real-world constraint with what the graph can represent (e.g. a quantity that cannot be negative). May combine writing, graphing, and reasoning about the solution set in one item.
constraints: Two-sentence real-world scenario; student isolates variable and boundary
Requires correct symbol, correct circle type, AND correct shading direction together
May involve a constraint where context limits meaningful solutions (e.g. $w \ge 0$ alongside the written inequality)
May ask the student to both write the inequality and describe/graph its infinite solution set

_difficultyRamp: The single ramped worksheet runs Easy (items 1 to 5) into Medium (items 6 to 11) into Hard (items 12 to 15). If split: tier1 covers Easy to Medium (strict and inclusive translation plus basic graphing), tier2 covers Medium to Hard (negatives/fractions, contextual extraction, combined write-and-graph reasoning).

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats the inequality as having one solution like an equation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answers that $x > 5$ means $x = 6$ (a single value) instead of infinitely many values greater than $5$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reverses the inequality symbol direction
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Writes $x < 48$ for 'at least $48$' instead of $x \ge 48$, confusing which way the symbol points

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses strict and inclusive symbols on boundary phrases
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Writes $x > 48$ for 'at least $48$' (which excludes $48$) instead of $x \ge 48$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses the wrong circle type when graphing
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Draws a closed circle for $x > 3$ or an open circle for $x \ge 3$, mismatching the boundary inclusion

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student shades the number line in the wrong direction
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Shades to the right for $x < 3$ instead of to the left, ignoring which values satisfy the inequality

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student includes the boundary value as a solution for a strict inequality
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says $x = 3$ is a solution of $x < 3$ because the number $3$ appears in the inequality

_comment_itemCounts: lesson 5+5, single ramped worksheet of 15 (tier1/tier2 available if split), quiz 8. Quiz items are multiple choice with LaTeX options and solution.steps.
